sentences.text: Mid Wilshire, Mid City.
This meeting is being recorded.
Ah, nice.
Yeah, we was there for six months about two years ago.
Manhattan Beach.
That's nice.
It was very nice.
Yeah.
But it took too long for our visas to arrive unfortunately, so we, we ended up coming back to the uk.
Ah, well, what part?
Well, we, we are London based but we live out in Somerset.
Do you know the UK very well?
Not very well.
I know certain parts of it.
It's the Southwest.
It's basically where all the pirates are from.
People that talk like that are who are.
That's funny.
Well, thank you for booking in some time with me and we can, we can really make this work.
I've had a good look around your site, so.
And your social media stuff.
So don't feel the need to give me like too much history because these sessions aren't really long enough.
You know, we run out of time before you know it.
But obviously it would be a good place to start to get a bit of history and what you're doing.
But really what I want to get into is, you know, where you feel the problems have been more recently and where the bottlenecks in the business are.
And obviously a good sort of thing to get into is why, why now?
Why do you think things are going to turn around and what's the, the strategy, that sort of thing.
So that's kind of the, the plan and then we can get into maybe some solutions how we can get more value out of the business.
And I think ultimately your goal is to sell, isn't it?
In a few years.
I noticed you've been on our mailing list for a while and you've done valuations on various forms that we have on the site and stuff.
So I guess in the back of your head you're thinking, how do I make this worthwhile to sell and exit so we can get into all of that as well.
But yeah, be great to know more about your history, just a little bit about me.
Obviously you're on our mailing list, but I'm the CEO of Capital A, we're an M and A advisory for marketing services.
All of our clients are either marketing agencies or buyers of marketing agencies.
So it's sometimes investors, private equity and stuff like that.
So yeah, how did you get into all of this?
I read on your.
Somewhere in your bio it might be your LinkedIn where it said you started something with Prince.

Yeah, well, I had been working initially in content delivery, so back then it was the format wars, you know, Windows media from Microsoft versus Reels RealPlayer and Apple QuickTime and as a delivery provider, largely Switzerland across those formats.
And then Apple came to me and said, hey, we like what you're doing with QuickTime, but we have an artist that wants to do this themselves.
And I said great, who is that?
They told me he was Prince.

And I got introduced to somebody on his team and you know, I was specializing at that point in anti piracy, digital rights management, content protection, which is still 20 years later, very hard to explain.
So to shorten that, I just took a file of Purple Rain and I encrypted it and I sent it back over to his team.
So when you went to play it, it said you have to be authorized, that is pay for it or be a member of his online fan community.
And got this email back in the middle of the night that says princess, this is exactly what I want to do.
And I was spelled eye and it was the numeral two in to do.
And quickly struck a deal and built the first real direct to consumer music service by a major artist.
And then added a ticketing component because he wanted to take, he's going to go on this massive comeback tour and sell the seats around the round of his symbol directly to the fan community.
So I got this quick kind of baptism by fire about what a live experience was.
I got to go see him do some tune up shows ahead of this tour.
And at the time I took over a boutique live streaming company.
So it was the Prince Experience, this boutique company that I had been advising for six or eight years and that was, I think I had 141 days on the job and that was bought by AEG.
And the other, the third pillar there was, I had started a dialogue with YouTube about why they wanted, why they should get into live video.
You know, one to bring flashed audiences to the platform and once the event is over, they could expose the audience to all the related video that lived across the YouTube ecosystem.
So I piloted a project with American Express that YouTube liked and they said you were right the way you did this.
We had a happy audience, we had happy music artists and we had happy brand in American Express.
We want to be in this business, but we don't do live today.

So for the next three or four years I powered everything on YouTube in addition to my customers which were Grammys, Oscars, Masters, TED conference, E3 live events and then everything on YouTube, Coachella, Bonnaroo, Rock and Rio product launches, movie premieres.
So it was really that Prince, AEG, YouTube.
And then it got.
It dawned on me that the world wasn't going to be just YouTube or just AEG.
So I exited and I formed this business.

I took a couple of key people with me and then I brought over Live Nation executive and I was early, well questioned and I thought, you know, we were killing it with anything that happened on YouTube and brands.
But because I was early, you know, I got into the space because of Mark Cuban.

I decided to go talk to brands and just listen and they told me we've got this recurring challenge of cord cutting, brand safety and ad blocking combined with this notion of how do we reach this younger consumer who's fueling this experience economy.

So I built a business that would address those things and over time got into, you know, client relationships with Coke, Jeep, Nissan, Hyundai, Amex, Coca Cola, Netflix, AT&T, ET cetera and built, you know, pretty successful business.

I haven't had to take on any investments largely because, you know, my sales training and background, you know, out of college I worked for NCR and you know, bigger, bigger companies as well as some mid tier ones and not delusional.

We're certainly a niche part of the online video space and it's had its moments certainly with the pandemic and then it kind of right sized and you know, so right now I'm not sure what I want to do but I believe there is an intriguing.
I've had to recalibrate the business a little bit to address this shift with brands to almost entirely on performance based marketing.
Right.
That's not enough for them to be powering something.
They need to achieve a call to action or a conversion.

So I spent the last 10 months becoming a TikTok shop certified agency and again probably a little early because we're on the live side of shop which as you probably know, TikTok shop and in general commerce means a lot of different things.
It's representing creators, it's short form video, it's media investments.

But what I'm seeing is that TikTok is going to prioritize live across the board at a higher quality of video and audio to bring more brands onto the platform and go beyond apparel, beauty and home goods.
So that is a different business in certain ways.
But it's also a parallel.

You know, if I've, my thinking is I've been, if I've been able to penetrate some of the biggest brands in the world and get either an MSA in place or preferred vendor status, I should be able to seize this opportunity when it starts to come to fruition for Live probably later in the year probably another quarter, maybe two.
So as a result, you know, I was operating a business that was consistently doing a million dollars in EBITDA the last two years it's been nowhere near that.
You know, had a big deal with Apple.
Apple brought it in house.
I was doing very well with AT&T when they were in their 5G marketing strategy that obviously has ended.
Rumors are that they're going to start marketing 6G but so I'm a little, you know, subject to some fluctuations in the market based there.

But I'm cautiously optimistic about what's possible with E commerce live streaming given that it's a you know, 400 billion dollar business in China and Tick Tock is I think done 23 billion this past year in the US and they've only really been a service for two years.
So.
That's kind of where I find myself.
I've been able to remove a lot of cost from the business and you know, candidly I've relied very heavily on my ability to drive a sales campaign and bring bring things to closure.
So.
So can we just get into to the numbers then?
Yeah.
So you said you did 1 million EBITDA.
So what's sort of the last seven years look like?
So maybe pre covered 2019.
Do you know that far back?
I do, I was just looking at that.
When was the golden years, John?
I would say 22, 21, 22 and 23 were probably those million dollar plus EBITDA years and then the last two we've now we're down around 500k in revenue.
So.
What was the revenue during those years?
21, 22, 2321 was 3.7 million.
22 2.9, 23, 2.9 and then we went down to about 482 and 24 and 448 and 25.
So what was 25 for?
448, yeah.
What was 1920?
Was that 19803?
Okay.
So 20 was really part of the golden golden years too.
And so post Covid it obviously.
Well it peaked during I guess and then for a couple of years after.
What do you think killed it in 23?
Were you hit by any of the writer strikes or anything else?
Was there any budget cuts because of that?
What did you see there?
We built Apple's Apple Music TV channel and that was incredibly profitable because it was largely a supposed to be an OTT cloud based solution for for some reason Apple.
We built it so quickly that we couldn't get approved by their engineering.
So they had to downlink it in a noc, which ironically was my old company's noc.
Long and short of it is they were able to bring that video and I'm surprised they outsourced to begin with, but that was super profitable, almost passive income.
Second was we were doing about 1.1 million with AT&T around their 5G marketing.
This was doing 10 pole executions at the NBA and WNBA all star game, the final four and the college football playoffs.
So big kind of multi day music experiences that we captured, filmed, produced, built microsites and helped them really tell their 5G, you know, marketing story.
And then that back then, you might remember, we've been advertising that 5G was people burning money between Verizon, T Mobile and AT&T across the board.
So those were two somewhat noteworthy changes that led to the, I'd say consolidation in our revenue and profit.
How many headcount did you have during those peak years and what have you got at the moment?
We were up around five to six and now we're down to three.
And that includes you?
It includes me, yeah.
Wow.
It's a, it's a really small team for that revenue.
It's pretty good.
Well, it's event based.
So, you know, if I'm going to do a, you know, music festival, I'll have a crew of 47.
But they're freelancers.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Okay.
All right, that makes sense.
Okay, so you said that you built Apple Music's TV channel.
So what is it that you guys actually do?
Because it sounds like it's way more technical than I was thinking.
We do three things.
So one, we provide all the live, live multi camera video production.
Could be four camera, it could be six, could be eight.
Some clients provide that rarely.
I mean everybody can quote film video, but live, live multi camera is pretty, just pretty rare, pretty unique.
I'm largely using production teams that I vetted and people cre over the last 20 years.
So I know I.
And I have the advantage of also having people in cities spread across the country and slash the world.
So I'm not loading up a plane in LA and flying it to Miami for Art Basel.
I'm sourcing gear, crew and equipment there.
Second, we provide all the technical services.
So things like, you know, taking the video from glass to glass from wherever it is from the filming and now rendering it onto a stream.
So that's video transmission and live encoding.
A lot of those.
Some of the times we're doing it on premise.
Sometimes we're using A cloud based capability, again largely a service, but we're probably the most experienced in the world at doing that.
And then third is distribution.
So based on who our customers are, we're sending this video to their either YouTube, Facebook, Twitch, Twitter, LinkedIn, Instagram or TikTok.
Or sometimes it's multiple platforms and sometimes it's multiple accounts.
We can also build bespoke microsites if needed.
So someone might say, I know I need to be on YouTube, but I want to own a relationship with the consumer.
And sometimes we're doing all three of these things together.
And then we've also built partnerships that allow us to have do audience development.
We can syndicate video through third party partners and drive viewership in that regard.
But it's really those core three capabilities.
Okay, so in terms of the Apple contracts, what did you specifically do for those guys?
Was that the technical services layer?
Yeah, so you built out all of their encoding so they could distribute across their own platform?
Yeah, so we basically ran channel that had about 9,000 music videos for the music industry.
And these were all was called Apple Music tv.
I think it's still operable today.
And you know, Justin Bieber might have a new music video coming out so we had to auto detect where his old video was in the channel and allow, you know, Apple to pull that one down and replace it.
Or if they had a, a takeover with say Bruce Springsteen.
So for the, for 12 hours they're gonna make it all Bruce and for two hours they're gonna interview him, he's also gonna perform.
But it was a complimentary channel to their listening audio service as well.
So it had like playlisting software built in somehow.
Yeah, exactly.
Okay, that sounds amazing.
And so how did that come to an end?
Because I think Apple had quite a few contracts that they brought in house over that period.
Well, it's funny, they have always said they don't get out of bed unless it's a billion dollar opportunity to bring their house.
But they actually ended up aggressively hiring video engineers.
A couple guys that I used to work with.
So I kind of knew the writing was on the wall and I was shocked that they were outsourcing this to, you know, just to begin with because they run Apple TV and Apple TV plus.
And I don't think it was that difficult for them to run this channel themselves.
And eventually they came to a decision where that, where they could.
We still were doing one off live, you know, projects for them, but they were very reliant on Twitter.
And Twitter's new ownership is Not a lot of brands have pulled back from broadcasting on Twitter, but that was it.
The bottom line was they had the ability to bring it in house and they did.
Okay, so tell me about you, John.
And I mean, sort of you personally, you strike me as somebody that could be quite a rebel, maybe somebody that can't be employed by anybody else.
And so you've always struck out on your own.
With you in charge, is that accurate?
I guess you could make that, make that assessment.
I mean, I am, at the end of the day, I think I'm really a salesperson.
I'm not a technologist per se and I enjoy listening to customers.
I don't tend to preach to them.
And what I'm trying to do is help get to, hey, how do I help solve your challenges and your problems?
You know, I've worked for a Fortune 100 company for six years, so I've had that experience.

Obviously I worked AEG, I think is around 20,000 plus employees, but I've also worked for mid tier companies, but I've been tagged with the serial entrepreneur handle for the last 20, which I'm happy to do, but I'm fairly flexible.
I can work in almost any environment, work from home, work in an office.
That doesn't really phase me either way.
But I do like to be empowered to identify an opportunity, run a sales campaign and bring it to closure.
I think I'm, I've, I've certainly identified that skill set.
I'm capable of it.
Yeah.

I think over my career I've been frustrated sometimes with management who doesn't understand that, doesn't understand how to get into a Netflix and get a win inside there or certainly an AT and T. So a lot of the companies I've worked for previously, I was their representative really in la, and I'm engaging the content community, whether that's brands, whether that's broadcasters, movie studios, record labels, or the general platforms themselves.
My preference has been to manage that communication and win that business.
But, you know, as long as there's good culture, I think I can be happy anywhere.
Okay, so you're really the sales guy that's, that's able to bring in the business and then you just share that around your team and get on with the next deal.
Precisely.
Yeah.
Okay.
And then just like your personal aspirations, what are you looking to achieve going forward?
You know, is, I guess we're probably around the same age.
So do you want to get out in the next five to 10 years?
I mean, I really like what I do.
Obviously I don't like the unpredictability of the event world and I've counteracted that by winning bigger deals.
I think we've done 21 projects lifetime with like AT&T or annually.
Every year we do Qualcomm's major Snapdragon summit experience from Maui.
Right.
That's their critical communication platform ahead of the Mobile World Congress or ces.
So but the, you know, if I were talking to an investor, you know, they're all about monthly recurring revenue and in the event based world that's really not how it operates.
But I've been able to maintain a pretty good level of profitability in my deals.
I'm happy to continue doing what I'm doing but yeah, sure, I'm not, not 29 or anymore.
And that's where I mean I, I have, you know, personal things.
I do play a lot of competitive baseball.
I want to continue to do that.
But I, I am intrigued by the, the E commerce aspect of my industry right now.
It's pretty, pretty interesting and have a little bit of an advantage there because most of the agencies in the TikTok shop world have, they had to do all the other things.
They know how to represent creators, they know how to do short form video and they how to do some media buying.
But I'd say 99.9% of them do not understand how to properly execute a premium live experience for a brand or an agency.
So I'm intrigued by that.

But I think what prompted me to have this conversation was I am also intrigued by, I'd like a little more stability but what I do want to do with my business is bring it back to a million EBITDA or hopefully get it to 2.
And you know that's going to take some work but I've done that before.
I'm pretty sure I can do it again.
Especially now armed with a better broader understanding of how E commerce works which has certainly been a learning process.
It's taken some time, it's certainly taken some time away from driving other businesses but the knowledge and the promise I think has been pretty compelling.
Okay, so what's the number that's driving this 1 or 2 million EBITDA?
What's in the back of your head?
As in, you know, I want to get to 1 million EBITDA because that gives me this kind of exit.
What, what are you thinking is the type of exit I want?
Well, I consume a lot of like your newsletters and just others in general.
And you know, I get it, there's got to be A floor, right.
No one's going to want to buy something that's way too negative.
So that's been one thing.
And you know, as I said, I've done this before in the prior years.
There's no reason why it can't be done again.

And you know, candidly, a lot of people and I've seen are out of business and fortunately I was able to run a business cost efficiently and save some dough from the bigger deals we did to keep us going and get to that adage of try to go skate to where the puck is going versus where it is.
And I think we have a pretty.
I'm intrigued by where things are lining up in that commerce world and certainly the other part of that is discovery.
And the other thing is I'm convinced that Amazon, Google and Meta are not going to let TikTok run away with this market.
And I have either MSAs or preferred vendor status with almost all of them.
So in some ways we're not even scratching the surface of what we could be doing.

I've also contemplated some capital just to build an E commerce business as well and bring in because there's so much tech, or should I say there's so much talent available given to the widespread layoffs that have come out of both Amazon, Google and TikTok.
There's incredibly capable people available as well.
But then I'm always thinking, you know, everybody seems to want to work for 1099 as well, so there's that.
So you know, these, these are the things that go through my mind in the course of the day.
Yeah, sure.
In fact, well, let's talk a little bit about that as.
So I mean you've not had an, an incredibly massive team anyway, but you've only got two other people working for you at the moment.
What, what are those two roles?
One is technically his title is CTO and he's also really our head project manager.
So a little bit of a background in tech and in live video production.

So for example, when we power Snapdragon Summit for Qualcomm, I assign him that he runs that program for the three days and then the week or two leading up to pre planning in terms of testing, fulfillment, coordinating with the various team members on the Qualcomm side and also facilitating where those streams are going to be.
Are they going to be on YouTube, LinkedIn, et cetera.
So really a technical position and the other is really a part time sales and well, he's working full time but he's, I'm paying him part Time part time rates.
I thought you did the sales though.
So what does he do?
The.
He's doing the knowledge of.
Of TikTok shop.
So I would probably find the opportunities and pitch some of the brands both for Cold Start and for.
If they're super successful.
There's the data on E commerce is pretty, pretty amazing.
We can find Every brand doing $10 million in GMV on Amazon that doesn't have a presence on TikTok and that's who we pursue.
So he's running a lot of those reporting and coming and really becoming what the other guy is for the commerce side of the business operations procedure, you name it.
He's modern sales by the sounds of things.
Yeah, I guess you could say.
Oh yeah, yeah, sure.
Okay.
Right.
So.

It's just this I guess weighs on where you are at the moment but what are you paying these two guys?
What's the CTO game?

So he could make four to five thousand on a project.
In the case of Qualcomm I think we paid him out 15,000.
So a little bit of my approach here is to manage and you know, if, if I'm.

What would you say costs in a year?
So the, the past couple of years being very similar.
What would you say?
Typically he's taken of that in the.
Higher earning years I paid him around 150.

4 to 25 in production work.
Is he.

Like it's tough space right now.

Eighteen hundred a month.

Eighteen hundred.

Los Gatos.

Not cheap to live.
Wow.

Yeah, I think it's family members probably.
Okay.
Okay.

Yeah.

Right.

Okay, so, I mean, so we're, we're probably well away from the ideal take home that you would be expecting to get in a normal year at the moment, personally.
Yeah, but it's, I mean, just judging by what you've been saying, it sounds like you've got money saved up.
So you're not struggling, but you're not bringing in the amount that you would, would like at this point.
Correct.
Okay, so tell me more about the E Commerce idea.
What do you think the, the revenue is going to do once you start focusing more on the, the big brands?
And I'm guessing you're going after the big brands that you, you're used to working with.
I mean, you've got so many.
Your website's amazing.
Just looking through the brands you've been working with, you are top draw on every single brand.
There's not a single brand I've not heard of in there.
Yes.
So what would a typical contract look like?
Have you, have you landed any of these deals yet or you currently just in learning mode?
I can, can I share my screen?
I can kind of have a slide.
I built on this.
So one of the things I've, I've contemplated is a raise in this space.
And.
This is a model of E commerce.
This is in beta.
I haven't completely finalize this, but the idea would be this is a, again a market that has largely been.
Well, I'll use Tick Tock as an example.
They're going to do 23.
They did 23 billion in North America in this past year after launching in September of 23.
And you know, the thesis is that pretty much any, anybody under the age of 40 is now largely buying through an E commerce mechanism or model.
58% of millennials have adopted this purchase behavior and 80% of Gen Z.
And it also is getting about a 30% conversion.
And traditional commerce e commerce is around 2 to 3%.
It also allows for decrease in returns of about 40%.

So having said that, we're anticipating that this space is going to mushroom beyond beauty, apparel and home goods into things like electronics where you want to show my Apple watch from different angles.
I can ask questions and talk about what colors that comes in.
And our thesis here is that we would set up studios.
I mean the theory is that retailers are going to.
Because the cost of running their retail business is so high.

Retail storefronts are going to become studios Monday through Friday where employees and creators will entertain the audience and sell product and they'll go back to traditional retail on Saturday and Sunday.

So I've modeled some thinking around higher tier clients that would, let's say Procter and Gamble that would require require us to build studios for them maybe at their headquarters or at their flagship store like the Tiffany on fifth Avenue or maybe it's the Grove in la.
Or we could run these experiences for them or they could come to a facility that we designed as well.
And these bigger entities, we'd have the benefit of getting paid for services.
But the beauty of TikTok shop agency ecosystem is we get to take a cut of everything that's sold.

So ideally we're either retained or a blend of retainer and service at 25k per month plus a 5% commission on what is sold through these systems in addition to maintaining our, our existing core business for amplifying experiences or what we've done historically with again att and Qualcomm, etc.
Do you think that's realistic getting commission from these really large brands?
Because surely they could just pay anybody to build the studio and then cut them off at that point rather than having, you know, a revenue that they can't control.
What is it about the, the experience that you're providing that you're going to be able to leverage that percentage as well?
It's kind of the, the formatting of the TikTok shop ecosystem.
In fact, do you provide the talent or what is it exactly?
No, the.
We provide the.
Well first you.
The way to.
You have to be bound to your seller.
And for most of these companies, in fact they don't want to do this themselves.
And I can certainly say based on 20 years of live streaming that nearly no one wants to manage that technology in that business.
In fact, some of my clients are actual production company.
They're BET is a client of mine.
They make content and we do the BET Awards they want nothing to do with live, live multi camera signal transmission, live encoding, publishing into YouTube, etc.
And the.

So to answer your question, the way this is architected is it is all agency commission based relationships And I believe TikTok requires that the sellers, the brands themselves have an agency relationship or this whole ecosystem would have a terrible time scaling and running efficiently.
We have to be as certified agencies cognizant of everything, fulfillment solving violations.
We use TikTok as an example.
You can't say the words weight loss like they can't in text or in verbal.
So it's things like managing and enforcing those things.
Also running the live streams.
I mean they, you know, Crocs was live every day in October.
They called it croctober.
They need my, they need people to do that type of work.
You provide the talent so you pull the whole thing together, including bringing the on screen talent.
Yeah, I mean we can.
I think that that market is way oversaturated and I'm already seeing TikTok starting to align the creators with the product they're experts at.
So there are some creators, there are creators everywhere and they're running into problems with like efficacy of them just taking free samples and not making videos on behalf of the brands.
And a lot of this is becoming automated and a lot of the audience is now they feel more trust with the brand directly than they do the creator.
So there are agencies out there that we could partner with to bring in the creators.
But TikTok is making that also an automated process.
You could just go into the dashboard of TikTok shop and say, hey, my client's Andy and he's in the fishing lure business.
I need to identify 20 creators that have at least 10,000 followers that also have generated an average of $6,000 a month in GMV.
So I necessarily don't need to go out and find these people.
I can just find them through that type of a research.
Could you just explain then how you are sort of improving the quality of the stream on behalf of these high quality brands?
If at the end of the day the creators end up, do they come to your studio at that point?
Is that how you, you would get it?
Yeah.
So this is an illustration.
What is happening is majority of the content on TikTok is underwhelming audio, very poor video and it's also poorly lit.
And I used, I thought a year ago, oh, I can just run in there and tell TikTok that if they elevated the quality of the video and the audio, they're going to sell more.
And I realized I'm one person trying to tell them that they need to learn this themselves.
So now they're getting data and feedback that when in fact they do take that route, there's more people watching and there's more conversion.
And this, if you can see the image is the old way or the 1.0 is a creator selling something, lipstick, say in their bedroom.
And last month or the month prior, Kim Kardashian launched skims on TikTok with a well produced, high quality broadcast that entertained the audience versus just heavily pitched.
And they got, I think she did 127000 in sales in 25 minutes.
So how did, how did she do it?
So she did it from a built studio.
I think she paid a TV company who's yeah, way crazy expensive and I'm, you know, we can deliver TV quality at a much more affordable price.
But have you been in touch with Kim?

summary.short_summary: John Petrocelli detailed Bulldog DM's financial trajectory, highlighting a decline in revenue from $3.7 million in 2021 to approximately $482,000 in 2024 due to losing key contracts with major clients like Apple and AT&T. Despite this downturn, the company remains debt-free and has streamlined operations with a lean team of three, primarily utilizing freelance staff to control costs. John is pivoting the business towards the burgeoning live streaming e-commerce market, particularly through TikTok Shop, which saw significant sales growth in 2023. He seeks $10 million in investment to expand into this space, targeting a potential $60 million business, and is considering a roll-up strategy to consolidate smaller firms for enhanced growth. John's focus on sales and client relationships positions Bulldog DM for future success despite current challenges.
